evidence.title: Predicting the Value of Radiology Artificial Intelligence Applications: Large-Scale Predeployment Evaluation of a Portfolio of Models
evidence.effect: Predeployment value predictions agreed with postdeployment survey respondents for 10 of 12 clinical tasks.
evidence.quote: Perceived value categories agreed between survey respondents and workgroup predictions for 10 of 12 tasks.

commentary.bottom_line: One prospective study in a real deployment of 88,645 examinations found that predeployment value predictions agreed with postdeployment survey respondents for 10 of 12 clinical tasks, which suggests a structured predeployment assessment may anticipate perceived benefit. No study tested whether a documented risk-benefit assessment linked to mitigation controls reduces errors or patient harm.

perspectives.view: A single prospective study with a comparator tested one component of this practice, which is predicting value before deployment. The outcome was agreement with clinician survey responses rather than harm. The risk, residual risk, and mitigation components went untested, and no second study confirms the finding. Indirectness and imprecision leave certainty very low.

The study compared predicted benefit with perceived benefit. It did not examine whether predeployment analysis of error severity and detectability identified the failures that later occurred, or whether linked controls caught errors before they reached patients. Disagreement on 2 of 12 tasks suggests that predeployment estimates may miss some effects.

The prediction step was carried out within a real deployment covering 88,645 examinations, which suggests it can be completed as part of routine governance. The study does not report staff time, the assessment method, or how consistently teams applied it, so burden and fidelity remain unknown.

The study did not report patient population characteristics. Whether predictions held for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients is unknown, and benefit and error severity may differ in these groups.

FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled device software asks sponsors to document and address misuse risk, and Utah HB 452 requires identification of foreseeable adverse outcomes for mental health chatbots. These provisions place risk documentation duties mainly on developers. No study measured whether health system assessments improve compliance or outcomes.

commentary.research_gap: Studies should test whether a documented predeployment risk-benefit assessment, with error severity, detectability, and residual risk tied to specific controls, predicts postdeployment errors and harms, and whether it changes deployment decisions or patient outcomes compared with deployments made without such an assessment. These studies should report staff time, patient demographics, and payer mix.
commentary.underserved_note: The one test of the practice did not report its population, so no evidence shows whether predeployment assessments were accurate for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Governance bodies cannot assume that the 10 of 12 agreement applies to these groups.
